entries.clue: Some baby's malodorous crap (7)

indicatorNotes.Some: only some of the letters of the following words are taken

blocks.note: the letters run on from the end of the first word into the start of the second

annotation.surface: A parent faces a truly foul nappy.
annotation.walkthrough: The nappy picture hides that 'crap' is an adjective here, meaning very poor, and the answer runs straight across 'baby's malodorous'.
annotation.definitionFit: Crap is British slang for dreadfully bad, a plain synonym in informal register.

entries.clue: The woman would – for Slough! (4)

blocks.note: the contraction of would after a pronoun, as in I'd or you'd

annotation.surface: A woman is willing to do something for Slough, the Berkshire town.
annotation.walkthrough: Slough looks like the Berkshire commuter town, but it is the verb, what a snake does to its old skin; the two pieces read together as she'd.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a snake sloughs its skin in the same sense.

entries.clue: One politician finished his shift bankrupt? (10)

indicatorNotes.shift: to shift letters is to move them into a new order

annotation.surface: An MP clocks off at the end of a working day, wondering whether he is broke.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Shift' reads as a work shift; it is the instruction to rearrange HIS. 'Bankrupt' is the verb, to make someone poor.
annotation.definitionFit: Used as a verb, bankrupt is a plain synonym, meaning to reduce someone to poverty.

entries.clue: see 18ac.
US writer getting end away? Lecher! (4)

indicatorNotes.getting end away: the last letter is sent away

blocks.note: Tom WOLFE, the American novelist, without his final E

annotation.surface: An American author has a sexual encounter and is branded a lecher.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Getting one's end away' is British slang for having sex, which is why the surface calls him a lecher; in the wordplay it only drops the last letter.
annotation.definitionFit: An informal sense: the word is slang for a man who predatorily chases women.

entries.clue: Hunt no longer takes opportunity to stagger back (10)

annotation.definitionNote: the definition describes the answer as a role Jeremy Hunt has left: it is the office Hunt no longer holds

blocks.note: to roll = to stagger or lurch; ROLL turned round

annotation.surface: A fox hunt has been banned, so its followers seize any chance to reel home drunk.
annotation.walkthrough: Hunt is Jeremy Hunt, the Conservative who ran the Treasury, the UK finance ministry, until the 2024 election, not a fox hunt.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by topical reference: Jeremy Hunt lost the finance minister's job in July 2024, so the title is what he no longer is.

entries.clue: It's not tender, filthy lucre today, on vacation (7)

indicatorNotes.filthy: the letters are dirtied, mixed up
indicatorNotes.on vacation: the word is vacated, emptied of its middle

blocks.note: TODAY with its insides removed, leaving T…Y

annotation.surface: Cash is no longer legal tender, and money these days is off on holiday.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tender' looks like legal tender, which fits 'filthy lucre', but it means gentle; 'filthy lucre' is a stock phrase for money, split here into indicator and fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by opposite: tenderness is gentleness, and the answer is its antonym.

entries.clue: Arty, virile male, welcomes one after personal problem (8)

indicatorNotes.welcomes: the outer word takes the letter in
indicatorNotes.after: that part comes after the first

blocks.note: BO = body odour, the classic personal problem
a he-man is a virile male
I = one, taken inside HE-MAN after the M

annotation.surface: A macho arty type puts up with someone who has a hygiene issue.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue reads right to left: 'after' means the body-odour piece, though named last, comes first in the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an unconventional, artistic way of living.

entries.clue: Throttle head off Theresa? (6)

indicatorNotes.head off: the first letter is taken off

blocks.note: to smother = to throttle; SMOTHER without its first letter

annotation.surface: Someone wants to strangle Theresa May, the former Prime Minister.
annotation.walkthrough: Theresa looks like Theresa May, but the question mark points to the nun of Calcutta, Teresa (spelt differently), known by her religious title.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example, flagged by the question mark: the Calcutta nun's title comes before her name.

entries.clue: Habit of House leader to leave one on Jack's butt (6)

indicatorNotes.leader to leave: a word's leader is its first letter, and telling it to leave removes that letter
indicatorNotes.on: in a down clue, the first pieces sit on top of the last

blocks.note: MANOR = a house, with its first letter removed
the butt, or tail end, of JACK

annotation.surface: The Leader of the House of Commons has a habit of walking out and leaving someone in the lurch.
annotation.walkthrough: 'House leader' looks parliamentary, but House is a manor and its leader is its first letter. 'Habit' is the clothing sense, as in a nun's habit.
annotation.definitionFit: A habit is a garment, and this hooded weatherproof jacket is one, a definition by example.

entries.clue: Blue party – pathetic sort (5)

annotation.surface: A Conservative party full of losers.
annotation.walkthrough: Blue is the colour of the Conservative party, so 'Blue party' looks political; it splits into two separate pieces.
annotation.definitionFit: British slang for a pathetic, socially inadequate person, a regional informal use.

entries.clue: Call on criminal to guarantee funds won't be misused (4-5)

indicatorNotes.on: the first piece is followed by the second

blocks.note: to ring = to call on the phone
a fence is a criminal who handles stolen goods

annotation.surface: Someone phones a crook to make sure the money stays clean.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface puts a crook next to money, but 'criminal' is the dealer in stolen goods, and the definition is a finance term, not a crime.
annotation.definitionFit: A budgeting idiom: money protected by an enclosure so it can only be spent on its intended purpose.

entries.clue: Offensive type, Roger sags balls (9)

indicatorNotes.balls: to balls something up is to make a mess of it

annotation.surface: A rude joke about an ageing man called Roger.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Balls' looks like the body part, fitting the smut, but it is the British 'balls up', to botch or jumble. 'Offensive' means attacking, not rude.
annotation.definitionFit: Offensive in its military sense, attacking: the type who strikes first.

entries.clue: Grisly old farmhand – the death of you? (4,6)

blocks.note: a reaper cut corn by hand in the old days

annotation.surface: A gruesome old farm worker who might finish you off.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 'the death of you' is the figure of Death himself, the scythe-carrying harvester of souls.
annotation.definitionFit: Death personified comes for everyone, so the idiom 'the death of you' is read literally.

entries.clue: Happening straight before Truss's debut (5)

indicatorNotes.before: the first piece comes before the second
indicatorNotes.debut: a debut is a first appearance, so the first letter

annotation.surface: Something happened just before Liz Truss first became Prime Minister.
annotation.walkthrough: Truss is Liz Truss, the briefest-serving UK Prime Minister; her 'debut' is only her first letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an occurrence.

entries.clue: Minister 'B' caught in mid-denial perhaps (2,8)

indicatorNotes.caught in: the B goes inside the other letters
indicatorNotes.perhaps: the letters are one possible arrangement of the answer

blocks.note: anagram fodder with B inside, 10 letters; the hyphen is ignored

annotation.surface: A minister, known only as B, is stuck halfway through denying something.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' looks like a hedge but is the anagram indicator; the answer is the former Labour leader who returned to government in 2024.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: he became energy secretary in the 2024 Labour government.

entries.clue: Slim sort needs to accept sex is restrictive (6)

indicatorNotes.sort: the letters are sorted into a new order
indicatorNotes.to accept: the outer letters take the inner ones in

blocks.note: it = sex, as in 'having it', placed inside LIM…S

annotation.surface: A slender person must come to terms with sex being off limits.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sort' reads as 'type of person', but it tells you to reorder SLIM. The definition is a verb phrase in the third person.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym as a verb: whatever restricts something is setting bounds on it.

entries.clue: Big spender wouldn't text part absent member (6)

annotation.definitionNote: the definition is a description, 'what a big spender wouldn't do', standing for the verb

blocks.note: SCRIPT (a text) without PT, the abbreviation for part

annotation.surface: A free-spending MP would never skip his lines or his seat.
annotation.walkthrough: PT is the standard abbreviation for part. 'Member' is not a limb but an MP.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by contrast: to economise meanly is the one thing a lavish spender won't do.

entries.clue: (& 4dn.) Deputy leader of Alaska turned on crooked air marshal (6)

indicatorNotes.crooked: the letters are bent out of shape, rearranged

blocks.note: AK, the postal code for Alaska, reversed

annotation.surface: Alaska's deputy governor turns against a corrupt senior air force officer.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Leader of Alaska' pulls the eye toward the letter A, but 'Deputy leader' is the whole definition: the US Vice President under Biden.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by role: the Vice President is deputy to the President, the national leader.

entries.clue: Delay getting Bet screwed in bed (7)

indicatorNotes.in: the twisted letters go inside the next word

blocks.note: the sack = bed, as in 'hit the sack'

annotation.surface: A woman called Bet is having sex in bed, which holds things up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Screwed' plays on its crude sense beside 'in bed'; for the solver it only scrambles BET.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a hitch that holds up progress.

entries.clue: Primary fiasco – Democrat replaces Republican with massive erection (7)

indicatorNotes.fiasco: a fiasco is a mess, so the letters are messed up
indicatorNotes.replaces: one letter is swapped for another

blocks.note: D = Democrat swapped in for one R = Republican

annotation.surface: An American primary election goes wrong as one party displaces the other.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Erection' sounds rude beside the Cyclops smut, but here it just means a building.
annotation.definitionFit: Erection in its building sense: an Egyptian tomb is a huge constructed structure, a definition by example.

entries.clue: Sod the world! (5)

blocks.note: sod = turf, a clump of soil with grass

annotation.surface: An exasperated cry of 'to hell with everything!'
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sod' reads as the British curse ('sod it'), but it is a clump of turf.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: soil or turf, and the name of the planet we live on.

entries.clue: Soldier wants shag with one knocked out on a routine basis (9)

blocks.note: a regular is a professional soldier

annotation.surface: A soldier wants sex that leaves somebody flattened.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Shag' is British slang for sex; 'one knocked out' reads as a boxing knockout, but it drops the letter A.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: at fixed, habitual intervals.

entries.clue: City needs data on eastern state (6)

annotation.surface: A city administration asks for figures about an eastern country.
annotation.walkthrough: 'State' suggests a nation to match 'eastern', but it is a US state by its postal code; gen is British slang for information.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a Swiss city on the lake of the same name.

entries.clue: "Bastard party needs right bloke!"– right-wing Tory (9)

blocks.note: b, the polite printed abbreviation of bastard

annotation.surface: An angry cry that the rotten party needs a proper right-winger.
annotation.walkthrough: The first 'right' is wordplay; the second belongs to the definition. The answer is the hard-right former Home Secretary, Suella.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a Conservative MP from the party's hard right.

entries.clue: Speech on housing that sounds familiar (4)

indicatorNotes.housing: the words house the answer inside them

blocks.note: the letters straddle the two words, dropping the first two and the last

annotation.surface: A speech about the housing crisis sounds like one heard before.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Housing' looks like the policy topic, but it holds the answer inside 'speech on'.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: a sound heard again is, by definition, one you've heard before.

entries.clue: Flipping one-time great gets award (5)

annotation.surface: A washed-up star gets a lifetime award, to someone's irritation.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' reads as a mild British curse; it reverses the whole string. 'One-time' is split in two.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the British Academy's film and television prize.

entries.clue: Panic causes fellow to cover genital area (4)

indicatorNotes.to cover: in a down clue the first piece sits over the second

blocks.note: the lap, the area over one's genitals when seated

annotation.surface: A man suddenly panics and covers his crotch.
annotation.walkthrough: 'To cover' reads as modesty, but in a down clue it just places the F above the second piece.
annotation.definitionFit: An informal British sense: being 'in a flap' is being flustered.

entries.clue: Mediocre cheap housing place providing child care (6)

indicatorNotes.housing: the words house the answer inside them

blocks.note: the last three letters of the first word plus the first three of the second

annotation.surface: Substandard budget housing includes a nursery.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Housing' again looks like homes, but it holds the answer inside 'mediocre cheap'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain descriptive definition of a day nursery, the word borrowed from French.

entries.clue: Sun leaving out evil controller (8)

indicatorNotes.out: the letters are out of order

annotation.surface: The Sun tabloid drops a villainous puppet-master.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Leaving out' looks like omission, sending a solver hunting for letters to drop; nothing is removed, 'out' just rearranges LEAVING.
annotation.definitionFit: An eponym: the sinister hypnotist in du Maurier's novel Trilby gave his name to any manipulative controller.
